lessons.text: When work seems lost in a version-controlled project, look in the history logs that record every HEAD movement (such as the reflog) and in the stash before assuming it is gone, because commits made on a detached or temporary checkout usually still exist there.

Before resolving a merge conflict, diff each side against the common ancestor to see what each one intended, and do not assume either side is correct: test the resolved result against the spec or examples, then confirm that no conflict markers remain and that the merge is committed.

When a task requires a service to keep running, launch it detached from the shell with its output redirected to a log, then confirm it works by making a real client request against it, including an edge case such as a missing key, before declaring the task complete.

When the task says the project's tests must pass, run the whole required suite as early as possible without stop-at-first-failure flags, so every failure shows up at once while there is still time to fix them; never mark the task complete while a required test is still failing, even if you think the failure is outside the main scope.

Under a tight time budget, start slow work (installs, builds, a timed reference run of the original) in the background at once, logging output and taking stdin from /dev/null, and keep developing meanwhile. Install only what is needed, and poll the log and job state instead of waiting blindly.

When a hidden harness will call your function or run your deliverable, write your own driver that invokes it the same way across many random inputs plus edge cases (zero, extremes, boundaries), compares against a simple reference, and times it, before declaring completion.

When a solution works by filtering a candidate space down to one answer, check whether distinct candidates could be indistinguishable under your test (equivalent or symmetric solutions), and confirm the surviving answer is unique rather than trusting that the first survivor is right.

Inspect every artifact shipped with the task inputs (binaries, scripts, leftover sources), since a generator or reference is often present. Run it in a scratch dir to confirm it reproduces the given output exactly, then recover its logic via strings, symbols and disassembly rather than guessing.

Before building or running anything that might write over provided input files, back them up and work in a scratch directory, then reproduce the stated acceptance check locally (the exact build command, the exact size or format limits, and the scoring metric against the reference) before declaring completion.

When filling in placeholders such as admitted proofs, TODO stubs or skipped tests, verify both that the artifact builds and that no escape hatch remains, using the tool's own dependency or assumption report where one exists, rather than trusting a clean compile alone.

Make the final check exit 0 only when the result is correct: print OK from inside the check (or chain with &&), never as a separate trailing line. In expect scripts a timed-out expect continues silently, so add a timeout branch that exits nonzero.

When a build must carry a special property (coverage, soft-float, static linking), first grep the build's own option list for a built-in switch. Then don't trust a clean compile: exercise or inspect the binary (e.g. run it and confirm its runtime data files appear and parse).

To construct an object meeting a few numeric constraints over a huge space, use a small parametric family with as many continuous free parameters as constraints, solve with a root-finder, and assert the constraints within tolerance. If a discrete scan only gets close, add a continuous parameter.

After writing a result file, reload it in a separate fresh process and recompute every required property straight from the stated definitions, such as size, type, validity and target values, rather than trusting the variables that produced it.

When a requirement is ambiguous about exactly which part of your output is measured (which substring, which boundary, which convention), design so the constraint holds under every plausible interpretation instead of betting on one reading.

If a value you must satisfy is normally computed by a standard domain tool, use that tool: search the repositories first, since it may be one install away. If it truly isn't available, implement the published formula, validate it against inputs with known reference values, and state the parameters you assumed.

For filtering or sanitizing tasks, test both sides. Run a broad, known-adversarial corpus through the filter so every attack is neutralized. Also confirm benign input comes out unchanged apart from the preinstalled parser's own normalization, so over-stripping and additions get caught.

When an external verification oracle (a browser, emulator or driver) fails to start after a quick diagnosis, switch to a cheaper check you can actually run, such as inspecting the outputs directly, instead of spending the time budget fixing the oracle, and state in your summary which check could not be done.

When a full build is slow or flaky, build only the smallest target the required acceptance check depends on rather than the default everything-plus-docs target, run it in the background with a log you poll, and protect enough of the time budget to actually run that check; blocking retry loops on the full build can use up the whole session.

To read text hidden in geometric data (e.g. toolpaths), parse it into primitives, keep the relevant object via the file's own labels, and render an image. If it spans many layers or a tilted plane, project onto its best-fit plane (PCA), then flip or rotate until level and zoom on look-alikes.

When drawing or processing tens of thousands of primitives, use one batched or vectorized call (a collection or array operation) rather than a per-item loop of library calls, and if a run stalls past a short wait, interrupt it and switch approach instead of waiting longer.

When a task lists several required behaviours, exercise every one end-to-end the way a real caller would, even if a provided eval script passes, since it may cover only some. Have each step leave an observable effect (file, marker), check it, then revert temporary changes.

For constrained-edit puzzles, keep all chosen edits in one script that rebuilds the file from the pristine backup and runs the acceptance check. Loop over candidate edits (apply, measure, print a compact score), commit one improvement at a time, fixing the earliest failure first, then re-measure.

If a trial-and-revert loop is interrupted or times out, assume the working file may still hold a half-applied trial edit. Before finishing, diff the final file against the original backup at a fine granularity (for example word by word) and confirm that every change is one you intended and is allowed.

Run the task's exact commands verbatim from a neutral directory and from the project folder, since paths resolve relative to the cwd. If your deliverable misses inputs from elsewhere, also look next to itself. A provided program that only works from its own folder is its convention, not your bug.

When a task asks for a numeric sequence or function of an unbounded input, check large inputs against both implementations and against values you already know, and use arbitrary-precision arithmetic rather than fixed-width integers, so silent overflow cannot produce wrong answers.

Order your endgame: finish edits and stop jobs you started, then run the final verification as its own plain command after the last write, not chained with cleanup, edits or guard tests (test -s, command -v ...). Prefer the task's stated check run verbatim and unpiped; it must write nothing.

When a file was saved by a heavy framework that is not installed, look inside it first, since many such formats are just archives of pickles and raw arrays. Often you can decode it with the standard library, for example a custom unpickler that maps the framework's rebuild hooks to plain readers, instead of spending the time budget installing the framework.

When reimplementing a computation in another language, cross-check the result against an independent second implementation on the real input. Also run it under each plausible preprocessing convention (scaling, normalization, layout) to confirm the answer does not depend on an ambiguity you guessed at.

Before committing to a long blocking wait on an interactive or slow process (a VM boot, an expect script, a build), take a quick short-timeout peek at its output to confirm it is progressing and that the channel you are watching actually carries its output, then poll in short intervals, so a silent stall cannot use up most of the time budget.

When driving a guest system through a serial or other headless console, first confirm the guest is actually configured to print to that console (for example by capturing a screen image or checking the boot loader prompt) rather than waiting for a login prompt that may only appear on the graphical display.

If a required library or runtime crashes on import or fails to start, spend the remaining time trying to get a working copy before falling back to guesswork, for example a different release or build installed into a separate virtual environment. Do not stop early and submit unverified changes to accuracy-sensitive settings while time is still left.

When compiling legacy C with a modern compiler, use permissive flags (e.g. -std=gnu89, -fcommon) and replace stale libc prototypes with standard headers. Recompile with -Wimplicit-function-declaration and -Wint-conversion to catch 64-bit pointer bugs, then compare -O0/-O2 outputs.

When recovering a hidden secret (key, seed, parameter) from known input/output examples, accept a candidate only if it reproduces every known example. Then produce the final outputs with the task's own provided tool rather than a reimplementation, and spot-check that tool on a few known examples before writing the answer file.

When a search is too large to brute force jointly but splits into pieces linked by an equation, hash one piece and look up matches while enumerating the other (meet-in-the-middle), in compiled code. Use several independent relations as the match key so false matches stay rare.

When only a final linear stage may be adjusted on top of frozen components, compute the frozen features once and fit that stage in closed form (regularized least squares) rather than running an iterative training loop, then confirm by diffing every parameter against the original that only the allowed ones changed.

When testing code whose output is random, compare statistics to known truth with tolerances scaled to the standard error, then rerun under many seeds: a correct implementation's goodness-of-fit rejection rate should match the nominal level (about 5% at 0.05). A persistently higher rate suggests bias.

Before declaring completion, stop background processes you started that the result does not need. Leave files in the task's directories in place; clear only your own scratch files in /tmp, and only if they could interfere. If ps/pgrep/pkill are missing, read /proc/*/cmdline to find, confirm or kill processes by command line.

Before writing a script a checker will run, test which third-party modules are installed; prefer the standard library with a fallback to an installed CLI tool. If you also use an optional package, rerun with its import blocked to prove the fallback path, and check the required output prints.

If a runtime or tool needed to run or check the deliverable is missing, install it (the distro package for a library also pulls in its interpreter) and run every required invocation for real, rather than shipping something untested. Note any version mismatch in your summary.

When an optimization must reproduce the output of an original that is too slow to run, get the reference output by running the unchanged original in an accelerated scratch copy of the environment (for example a copied database with added indexes, leaving the provided original untouched), then compare your fast version's output byte for byte against it.

When transcribing logic or constants from an image or other lossy source, list the plausible readings of the ambiguous parts (look-alike characters, raw versus hex or encoded forms, lengths). Compute them all in one script and let any provided check value, such as a hinted prefix or a checksum, pick the right one, rather than committing to a single guess.

After building a compiler, interpreter or similar tool, drive it through the whole pipeline on a small realistic sample (compile, link, run and check the output), because a successful build can still leave runtime libraries or headers missing from the locations the tool expects.

When a file looks scrambled or encrypted, compare its first bytes with the format's documented magic header and look for long runs of one repeated byte (likely encoded zero padding); XOR often reveals a simple key. Confirm it by checking the decoded file passes the format's own integrity check.

Opening a file with its normal library can silently change it (checkpointing, merging logs, deleting side files, creating locks), so do the inspection and extraction on a copy, then make sure the delivered files are in the intended state afterwards.

When code was changed but no history or diff exists, find the bug by comparing the suspect routine with sibling routines that walk the same data structure; a step, bound or invariant that differs from its siblings is usually the regression. Check every walker for that deviation and fix each minimally.

When building an emulator, VM or interpreter, first disassemble the program and tally the instruction mnemonics to learn the exact subset used. Read any bundled source for how syscalls are numbered, since its wrappers may not follow the standard ABI. Implement that subset and fail loudly on anything else.

When a specific package version is required and building from source would be slow, install prebuilt binaries from a repository snapshot pinned to a date when that version was current, so its dependencies are matching versions from the same time rather than the newest ones; then load the package and print the installed versions of it and its key dependencies to confirm.

When an optional library setting changes the result, let the task's wording decide: if it names roles like a query and documents, use the library's role-specific mode (e.g. a query prompt in the model's registered metadata), even if it needs a placeholder argument. Else use the default.

Before writing code that transforms or merges data, print every input's actual contents and column types in one exploratory command, so that schema gaps get noticed and handled on purpose, such as a required field missing from one source or an equivalent field stored in a different type or encoding. State each mapping choice you made in your summary.

Before editing a service's configuration, read its top-level config file and follow every include, because a provided environment may define its own server blocks or upstreams that override the distro defaults. If a request then returns a proxy error, check which backend the active config actually points at, and adapt to it rather than assuming your edited file is the one in effect.

When booting a provided disk image, read the guest's own config straight out of the image first (userspace filesystem tools at the partition offset, or raw byte search) to learn which drivers and hardware it expects, then pick matching emulated hardware instead of cycling options.

When an answer depends on an eligibility filter (complete results, size limits, availability), print the top candidates both with and without the filter, together with the reason each one is excluded, so you can confirm the filter is what changes the winner and that no candidate was dropped by a loading or naming glitch.

When writing numeric data files for others to read, use an explicit plain format (one value per line, fixed decimals) rather than default printing, then view the first lines and re-read the file to check for padding, scientific notation or mixed formats.

When porting to a new major library version, find every import alias and check each aliased attribute use against the installed library's real namespace (e.g. an AST walk with hasattr), which catches removed APIs a grep list misses. Pin the existing version via a constraints file.

If the task invokes a program at a path where only its source exists, build it at exactly that path and run the stated commands verbatim there as the final check. Tests against a copy built elsewhere may not count as verifying the delivered state. Mention the extra built file in your summary.

When building old source with a newer packaged toolchain, try the build's own version-override option first. Then patch each identifier the newer toolchain removed to its documented replacement, one minimal edit per error, instead of building an exact older toolchain.

When your deliverable is an input to a downstream process you can model, write a simulator that reads only the delivered file plus the given inputs and reproduces the final target end-to-end; iterate until it matches exactly, since that catches orientation or ordering errors a checklist misses.

When the task hints that a secret comes from a small seed or a reduced space, enumerate that reduced space and filter candidates with cheap consistency checks against chosen or observed data, instead of attacking the full space.

When several unknowns are jointly too large to search, look for relations or checks that involve only one unknown at a time (e.g. outermost layers), filter each piece independently first, then search the remaining pieces conditioned on the few survivors.

When using a detector (browser, scanner, test harness) to prove that something harmful was removed, first confirm it flags each unfiltered positive control. Cases where the original never triggers prove nothing, so fix the trigger or verify those cases another way.

After the required tests pass, also run the few neighbouring test groups that stress the subsystem you changed. A fix can pass the required suite and still break a related path, and these runs are cheap extra confidence.

When no reference implementation can run, validate with a canonical input whose correct output is widely known, such as famous boilerplate text a model should complete, and also print intermediate values (token IDs, offsets) to compare against values you know are right.

When a binary data file has no index, first check that its size equals the expected element count times the element width, which shows it is raw and headerless. Then use per-segment statistics (scales near one, biases near zero) to infer storage order before writing the loader.

When a compiled program crashes or corrupts memory, rebuild it once with a memory sanitizer and debug info and rerun the same input. This points straight to the overflowing line and buffer, which beats guessing from the abort message.

Read the full output of a passing smoke test for warnings or fallback notices, such as a program reporting a degraded mode caused by an inherited environment setting. Fix the cause in your deliverable rather than accepting the side effects of a test that only happened to pass.

When the task names a specific version known to work and the packaged newer version misbehaves, switch early to that exact version, building from source in the background with a minimal target list if needed, instead of spending the budget on workarounds for the newer one.

When a service runs as a dedicated unprivileged user, run its admin commands as that user rather than root. Afterwards, search its data, log and run directories for files with the wrong owner, because root-owned files left behind by your setup can quietly break the daemon later.

When no C compiler is installed, first start the distro package manager install (minimal, no recommends) in the background while you explore. If that is unavailable, try a pip-installable toolchain such as the ziglang package, which bundles clang plus libc headers.

When the deliverable produces an image or other visual output, convert it to a format you can view and actually look at it. Check that the content is the expected scene, not just that the file exists with a valid header and size.

When a language's package manager normally compiles packages from source on Linux (R being a common case), point it at a prebuilt-binary repository built for your exact OS release. This turns long compiles into quick downloads; afterwards, print the installed version to confirm it matches the requirement.

For 'as of' a past date questions, check out the data's version-controlled source at the last commit before that date (shallow or sparse clone if large). Compute with the tool version released around then, reusing its own aggregation code instead of reimplementing it.

When recovering deleted data from a raw image, list byte offsets of each known piece separately (prefix, suffix, filename) plus the container's header signatures, since a full-pattern search misses split data. Hex-dump each hit, rejoin fragments, and accept only if a stored CRC or length matches.

When inputs include a list of identifiers or reference files, treat it as a candidate menu: look up each candidate's properties in an authoritative source and pick by matching the task's stated numbers/criteria, rather than choosing from memory.

When a model or classifier's output cannot be checked against a reference runtime, inspect the input yourself, for example by rendering a small image as ASCII art with a quick standalone decoder, and confirm the prediction matches what a human would answer.
When a task forbids modifying an input file, record its checksum before any work and recompute it in your final verification, so you can prove the protected file stayed byte-identical.

When rewriting code or a query to be faster but give identical output, first save the original's output as a reference. Query the data to confirm the invariants each simplification relies on (no orphan keys, uniqueness). Then byte-compare the new output, headers included.

Before analysing measured data, check that its axis lands known reference features (textbook peak positions, expected ranges) where they belong. If not, try plausible unit conversions or reciprocals and the locale's number format (such as decimal commas) until the known landmarks line up, then state the conversion you used.

When fitting a peak in a chosen data window, refit with narrower and wider windows. If parameters drift, use a wide window (many linewidths of baseline per side) where they level off, since narrow ones cut heavy tails and bias width/offset. Name the width/height convention.

When a hidden harness will load your deliverable (a pattern, config or script), mimic its exact consumption path: the same file read and strip, applied to the whole input with the same flags. If its runtime is absent, use a compatible engine and note it. Per-line or hand-pasted tests can disagree.

When writing a query or filter over a small provided dataset, work out the expected result by hand first, including near-miss records and why each is excluded (missing end dates, typos, boundary dates). Then run the query in a real engine and confirm the output matches.

To make a built tool available on PATH, link or install it into a standard bin directory that is already on the default PATH, rather than only editing a shell rc file. Then verify it resolves and runs from a fresh login shell started in an unrelated directory.

When tuning for speed under an accuracy tolerance, write a small harness printing max error vs the reference and the time ratio over several seeds. Sweep candidate settings in one loop (solver choices, disabling unused features), then pick a winner with margin on both and recheck on many seeds.

Before optimizing, use the tool's built-in profiler or timers to find which stage dominates the runtime, and also check which features are actually exercised (e.g. counts that stay zero). Then target the costly stage and switch off the idle features.

When installing a package with compiled extensions from source, also build them in place in the source tree. Then run the tests both inside the repo and on a copy outside it against the installed package, and compare compiled results with the pure-language fallback where one exists.

When a test fails inside code that consumes a third-party library's output (a missing key or attribute), probe the installed library with a tiny input and print the real structure, then patch the consumer to accept both old and new names rather than pinning or guessing.

Check the exit status of every successful run of a program you built, not just its printed output. Legacy code with a void main or no final exit can return a garbage nonzero status that callers read as failure, so make it exit 0 explicitly and recheck.

When the deliverable is a large machine-like artifact (a circuit, netlist, generated program or table), write a generator script built from small composable helpers and regenerate the artifact from it. A bug fix then becomes a one-line edit followed by a rerun of the full test sweep.

When generating an artifact for a strict consumer, put assertions in the generator for the consumer's structural rules (ordering or index constraints, size limits, no dangling references). A violated assumption then fails loudly at generation time instead of yielding silently wrong output.

When a search loop catches exceptions and then finds nothing, rerun a single representative case outside the try block with the full traceback shown. For root-finders, print the function's value at both bracket ends, because a hidden bad-bracket or domain error is often the real cause.

When both the inputs and the desired final result are given, first align or diff each input against the target to locate where every piece lands and what the junctions are; derive the design from that mapping instead of guessing, and keep the mapping script for the final end-to-end check.
When recovering an orphaned commit, create a named branch pointing at it before you merge or reset, so the work stays reachable even if the merge goes wrong or has to be aborted.

When editing by line number (e.g. with sed), print the surrounding lines right after the edit to confirm the intended line changed and nothing nearby got clobbered, since line offsets are easy to get wrong.

If you edit sources while a background build is running, rerun the build after it finishes so the final artifact includes every edit. For low-level fixes, also run a stress program under the project's own debug build with its built-in invariant checks turned on.

To prove a VM or GUI accepts programmatic input, capture the screen, send one harmless key or shortcut through the control channel, capture again and compare the captures. Then look at the image to confirm the expected reaction (e.g. a menu opened), and undo it.

After running a code generator or build step, list the files it actually produced before you reference them in your code, because tools often rename outputs, for example by replacing characters that are illegal in identifiers. Then import or use the real names.

Apply a prescribed setting only to the scope the task names. Do not copy the same value onto analogous sibling settings without testing each one end-to-end, since it can silently disable another stated requirement (such as a confirmation step). Explain any deviation in your summary.

For a long-running or never-exiting deliverable, measure how soon the required output appears. If a shorter run lacks it or it is incomplete, treat that as a defect to fix by cutting startup cost, not a quirk to explain away, since hidden checkers likely use modest timeouts.

When an answer comes from MCMC or another stochastic estimator, cross-check it with an independent deterministic method, e.g. integrate out nuisance parameters analytically and grid-integrate the low-dimensional marginal (include the Jacobian for log-spaced grids). Agreement confirms model and code.

When edits interact non-locally (one change reflows or shifts everything after it), stop greedy one-at-a-time fixes. Restrict to the affected region and, from a saved baseline, enumerate joint combinations of allowed choices (exhaustively if small, else randomly), ranking by the full check.

When a tool reports only failures, run a scratch copy with its diagnostics set to report everything (all lines and states, not only errors). That shows the context around the problem and which nearby choices actually affect it, while the delivered files stay unchanged.

When scripting languages and hex tools are missing, check which core tools remain before installing anything: perl is often present when python is not (its bundled zlib module computes CRC32), and grep -a -b -o for offsets plus dd and od for dumps cover most binary work.

When one source file must build and run under several toolchains or interpreters, compile it with every stated command verbatim and print the outputs side by side over a range of inputs, including edge cases and large values, so any divergence between the targets shows up at once.

When building a deliverable out of records fetched from reference databases, copy each record verbatim and apply only the exact edit the task prescribes. Trimming extra leading/trailing bits you judged cosmetic can break a checker that compares your output against the untrimmed reference.

When optimizing a query or pipeline that ends in a top-N limit, compute the cheap ranking aggregate once, apply the limit first, and only then run the expensive per-row work (correlated subqueries, lookups) on the survivors, keeping the original tie-break order exactly.

When the terminal may hide or truncate output lines, do not rely on reading test results by eye. Write the expected results to a file and diff the actual output against it, printing only OK or the mismatching lines, so every case is verified.

When a task gives a reference date and uses words like 'current' or 'active', apply that date to every time-bounded field in the data (start and end dates). Decide explicitly how missing dates are treated, and say in your summary which records the date filter excluded.

When your code rejects bad inputs with a validity check, run it across many seeds and extreme but valid inputs (far-off locations, tiny scales) to catch false alarms. Rare spurious failures often come from values near underflow, so leave numerically unreliable points out of the check.

Build the known-truth test suite to cover every code branch, such as bounded and unbounded domains or increasing and decreasing pieces. Then compare which cases pass and which fail: the property the failures share points at the branch with the bug, for example a sign error.

When a spec requires a check to fire at a specific phase (e.g. during processing, not just at setup), build a test input that passes the earlier phases and only violates later. Record that the violating path was actually reached, so the test proves the check works in that phase.

When building a source package whose compiled parts must match an already-installed dependency version, disable the installer's isolated build environment so it compiles against the installed version, not a fresh newest copy. Then print each extension's __file__ to rule out a silent pure-language fallback.

When a checker will compare your program's output to a reference, do not stop at a run that writes to a null sink. Write real output files, check their format and size and that the content is not trivial, and run the same input twice and byte-compare the results to confirm the output is deterministic.

When the real consumer is too slow for broad testing, write a fast independent emulator of it (e.g. bit-parallel, 64 cases per machine word). Test both ends of every piece of a piecewise target (floors, roots, thresholds), then confirm a sample on the real consumer.

After a numeric solver hits its target, rerun it on several other targets and sizes to expose fragile assumptions. If a bracketed root-finder then reports same-sign ends, step outward from the safe end to the first sign change instead of using extreme endpoints, where the function can turn around.

When each item of a deliverable must follow a prescribed layout, build them all with the same canonical structure and no extra filler elements; ad-hoc padding added to tune one item can make a positional checker misread which part is which, even if your end-to-end simulation passes.

When you reimplement a provided primitive (for speed or inlining), assert it equals the original on many random inputs before building on it. If an attack or algorithm that should work succeeds only sometimes or yields no candidates, suspect a copied-helper bug such as missing masking before doubting the method.

For a differential attack, trace the chosen input difference through the whitening, mixing and early rounds by hand. Look for one that passes deterministically (probability 1), so that every pair is a right pair and a single exact check can filter the last-round key candidates.

When a harness calls your function, keep it free of side effects on shared state. For example, use a private RNG instance instead of the global one, and in your test driver assert that the caller's global state (RNG state, cwd, env) is unchanged after the call.

Treat preinstalled packages as hints about the hidden checker. A browser driver suggests results are judged by executing them; a preinstalled parser suggests which normalization is expected, so prefer it over downloading a different library whose output differs.

When a task says output must match the input except for removing harmful parts, only delete. Never inject unrequested extras (new meta tags, added attributes, wrapper elements, hardening tweaks), and diff benign input against output to confirm nothing was added.

When looping a test or check command over several targets with filtered output, confirm each target printed its own summary. A missing one usually means the target name is wrong or nonexistent and nothing ran, so list the available targets and rerun the right ones.

When a crash happens deep inside a build, get the exact failing command from the build tool's dry-run mode and rerun it under a debugger for a backtrace. After fixing, prove the fix with a regression test that crashes on a saved copy of the old binary and passes on the new one.

To view a plot without an imaging library, try a quick pip install first (often seconds). If that fails, write a minimal grayscale PNG with only the standard library (zlib plus struct). Split long, wide renders into overlapping tiles so each one stays readable.

Compile with the task's exact stated command, keeping its argument order, from an unrelated directory. A library flag placed before the source file can fail to link. If you cannot change the command, change the code so it no longer depends on that flag's position.

When testing a terminal, REPL or other interactive driver, have each typed command write its result to a scratch file and check those files, because screen output mixes echoed input, prompts and escape codes. Back up any user config you temporarily edit to test it, and restore it afterwards.

When a deliverable spawns processes, threads or file descriptors, create and close it many times in a loop and assert that open-fd count, thread count and leftover child processes are unchanged. Include a child that ignores signals, so cleanup can't hang or leak.

When unsure which settings fix a failure, launch every candidate configuration in parallel as separate scratch instances, each with its own log or control channel, then compare results together. If all fail identically, those settings aren't the cause, so move on, e.g. to the version named in the task.

When an emulator or tool misbehaves in a specific way (missing graphics, ignored ops), turn on its built-in trace events or guest-error logging, trigger one small action, and read the source path that handles the logged operations. A minimal targeted patch then rebuild often beats cycling options.

Configure a service through its stock, documented settings and change only what the task asks for. Avoid custom plugins, monkeypatches or overrides of built-in behaviour, and leave no extra files in the task directory. A hidden checker may drive the system in ways your additions change or break.

Make the final check a fresh run of the user's exact command on the delivered artifact, judged by what that run itself produces. Assertions over logs, hashes or reports saved by earlier runs only show a past state and can hide a regression.

When your deliverable produces an output file that a checker may poll for or read while the program keeps running, write it to a temporary file and rename it into place, so the file is never seen half-written.

When a deliverable produces output (an image, a file) and no reference output exists, write a separate script that computes the expected result straight from the raw input assets and the source's own tables or formulas. Then compare byte for byte, rather than trusting a plausible-looking result.

After an MCMC or other iterative estimator runs, read its diagnostics (divergences, R-hat, effective sample size). If it warns, rerun with stricter settings (e.g. a higher acceptance target) and check that the estimates stay stable before writing results.

After writing a model in a probabilistic language, evaluate its log density at many random parameter points, boundary values included, and compare with an independent hand-coded density. The difference must be the same constant at every point, which proves the model code is right before you trust any sampling.

Before fetching from a bundle or remote, list its refs and the commit each one points to, since HEAD and a named branch can point to different commits (one may be only the shared base). Fetch the ref that holds the actual work, then view the commit graph to confirm.

When an installed library's loader always fetches the newest data, read its source to find the cache-directory setting and the no-update flag, then point it at your own pinned local checkout. That way the library's own parsing and aggregation run on the historical snapshot you chose.

Don't trust a precomputed index file or an API listing to be complete. If a listing reports truncation, or results seem sparse, list everything cheaply with a shallow, blob-less clone (ls-tree) and fetch only the files you need. A full listing can reveal eligible candidates the index missed.

For search-based fixing against a checker, score each trial by a graded value (number of violations weighted heavily, plus their total magnitude) rather than pass/fail. Try only edits near the reported violations, so the loop can accept partial progress and converges quickly.

Check the first easy hit (a grep match, an obvious file) against every property the task states, such as length, prefix, suffix and charset. If any one fails, treat it as a decoy or partial fragment and keep searching other offsets or copies rather than submitting it.

When a reimplementation's output nearly matches a reference, count the most common (yours, reference) value pairs among mismatches and print a coarse spatial map of where they differ. A dominant pair usually points straight at one wrong constant or branch, so it beats rereading the code.

When reimplementing a program from its disassembly, mirror its exact numeric types and conversions: float versus double, casts around library calls like sqrt, and the order of operations. Aim for byte-identical output and check it with cmp, not just approximate similarity.

When the task hands you identifiers or accessions, pull each record from the database those IDs index and use its content verbatim (expanding only placeholders it documents). A second database's entry for the 'same' thing can be a trimmed or variant copy that a checker won't match.

Run the final verification as a command whose own text shows the check (a named script or a one-liner, not a heredoc piped into an interpreter). Give it a long enough wait to finish in that same call, since a result collected later by polling may not count as verifying your last change.

When rebuilding an architecture from saved parameters, load with strict key and shape matching and regenerate deterministic buffers, comparing them to the stored ones within float tolerance. Sweep hyperparameters that leave no trace in shapes (e.g. head count) and report your choice.

To replace a correlated 'top item per group' subquery (order by count desc, id asc, limit 1), aggregate once per group and pack the sort key and the tie-break into one integer for MAX (e.g. count*BIG - id), then decode both parts arithmetically. Check that BIG exceeds the id range.

To prove a rewritten query or transform is equivalent, also diff it against the original on small synthetic fixtures that break the real data's incidental invariants (duplicate keys, ties, orphan references, empty tables), randomized over many seeds. Equivalence must hold for any data, not just this data.

For regexes consumed by findall, remember that capture groups change what is returned: use exactly one group for the wanted part and non-capturing groups elsewhere. Put line-wide conditions in a lookahead anchored at line start, and use a greedy prefix to pick the last occurrence.

When a randomized comparison against your own reference reports a mismatch, first check the failing case by hand against the spec, since the reference is often the buggy side. Fix whichever is wrong and rerun the full sweep, rather than reflexively bending the deliverable to match the reference.

If the package manager says it cannot locate a package in a fresh container, the package index is probably empty. Run the index update before the install, in the background with a log, rather than giving up on the tool or switching to manual workarounds.

When a faster algorithm or solver nearly meets an accuracy tolerance, tighten its own convergence tolerance or iteration settings and re-measure before discarding it. Extra precision is often cheap and buys a safe accuracy margin while keeping most of the speedup.

When only some settings of a config or model file may change, parse both the original and your edited version, remove the intended edits, and assert the remaining trees are identical. Also compare the compiled or loaded values of the protected properties, which proves nothing forbidden changed.
